title: Propositional logic: AND, OR, NOT, XOR, truth tables
story:
George Boole published An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, on Which are Founded the Mathematical Theories of Logic and Probabilities in 1854. It develops an algebraic treatment of logic in which the variables take only two values — so that reasoning about propositions becomes calculation, subject to laws that can be stated and proved like any other algebra.

The work did not sit untouched afterwards; mathematicians and logicians developed it throughout the following decades. What had not happened was the connection to machinery.

That came from Claude Shannon, who submitted A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits as a master's thesis at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 1937, published the following year in the Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers. The observation is exact rather than metaphorical: the algebra of two-valued logic describes the behaviour of relay and switching circuits precisely. Circuits in series correspond to conjunction — current flows only if both switches are closed. Circuits in parallel correspond to disjunction — current flows if either is.

Follow what that identification actually buys, because it is easy to nod at and miss. Before it, designing a circuit meant arranging switches until the behaviour looked right, and checking it meant testing it. After it, a circuit is an expression. You can prove two circuits equivalent without building either. You can simplify an expression by algebra and know the smaller circuit does the same thing — fewer relays, less cost, fewer parts to fail. The design problem became a symbolic one, which is what made it possible to design circuits far too complex to arrive at by arranging things.

The operations themselves are small enough to hold entirely. Conjunction is true only when both parts are. Disjunction is true when at least one is — note at least, since the everyday word usually means one or the other but not both, which is a different operation. Negation flips. Exclusive disjunction is the one everyday speech actually means by or: true when the two parts differ.

The laws worth knowing by name are the two that let negation move across a bracket. They are named after Augustus De Morgan, a contemporary of Boole's, who stated them in Formal Logic: or, The Calculus of Inference, Necessary and Probable, in 1847 — seven years before the Laws of Thought. The negation of a disjunction is the conjunction of the negations, and the negation of a conjunction is the disjunction of the negations. Both directions matter in practice, because a condition written as a negated compound is hard to read and easy to get wrong, and pushing the negation inwards usually produces something a person can evaluate at a glance.

One habit is worth more than any of these identities: when a condition has few enough variables, enumerate them. Two variables give four rows, three give eight. Writing out every case and its result settles an argument about operator precedence or an edge case definitively, in less time than the argument would take — and it is the only method that does not depend on the reasoner being right.

The cost of the whole arrangement is worth naming, because it is the reason everything else in computing looks the way it does. If the hardware can distinguish only two states, every quantity a machine handles has to be encoded as a pattern of them first. Numbers, text, images, sound: all of it is a convention layered over two-state storage, and most of the difficulty in the rest of this track comes from those conventions rather than from the logic, which is the part that is genuinely simple.

problem.name: Conditions as algebra
problem.shape: A decision depends on several conditions combined, and the combination has to be correct.

operator precedence is being relied on rather than parentheses
two conditions are believed equivalent and nobody has checked
problem.move: Treat the condition as an expression to be manipulated rather than prose to be read. Push negations inward across brackets so the operators are positive, and where the variables are few enough, enumerate every combination and its result instead of arguing about it.
problem.invariant: Two-valued logic and switching circuits are the same structure, so a condition can be simplified, proved equivalent and reduced symbolically without being executed.
problem.breaks: The algebra assumes both sides of an operator are simply true or false. Real conditions in code short-circuit, so the second operand may never be evaluated — which means reordering an expression the algebra says is equivalent can change whether a side effect happens or an error is raised.

cost.space: every quantity a machine handles must first be encoded as a pattern of two-state storage
cost.beats: reading the condition carefully, which is faster and depends on the reader being right, and testing it, which checks the cases you thought of

worked.problem: What are De Morgan's laws, and how do you rewrite the negation of a disjunction to remove the outer negation?
worked.reasoning:
They are the two identities that let a negation move across a bracket, changing the operator as it goes. The negation of a disjunction equals the conjunction of the negations: not one-or-the-other is the same as neither. The negation of a conjunction equals the disjunction of the negations: not both is the same as at least one missing.

So the negation of 'is an administrator or is an editor' becomes 'is not an administrator and is not an editor'. The outer negation is gone and each term is now directly readable.

Why this matters in practice is not elegance. A negated compound forces a reader to hold the inner expression in mind, evaluate it, and then invert the result — three steps, with the inversion applying to something they have just constructed mentally. Pushing the negation inwards makes each term a fact about the world that can be checked on its own, and the combination is then a single step. That is the difference between a condition people get right and one they argue about.

If the identity is not obvious, it can be verified rather than trusted, which is the habit worth having. Two variables give four combinations; write both expressions in all four and compare. That takes under a minute and settles it, which is generally faster than the discussion it replaces, and it does not depend on anyone's recollection being correct.

The same technique scales to the cases that actually cause bugs. Three variables give eight rows, which is still tractable by hand, and enumerating them settles arguments about precedence and boundary conditions definitively. Most disagreements about a compound condition are resolvable this way in less time than it takes to have the disagreement.

I would state the limitation, because the algebra is not quite the language. It assumes both operands are simply true or false. Real conditions short-circuit: if the first operand of a conjunction is false, the second is never evaluated. So an expression the algebra calls equivalent may not be equivalent in code — reordering can change whether a side effect happens, whether a null is dereferenced, or whether an expensive call is made. Applying De Morgan's laws changes the operator, which changes which operand guards which, and that is exactly where a mechanical rewrite can introduce a fault the truth table cannot show.

The underlying reason any of this is trustworthy goes back to the identification the field rests on. Two-valued algebra and switching circuits are the same structure — series behaving as conjunction, parallel as disjunction — so manipulating the expression really is manipulating the circuit, and a simplification really does produce something that does the same thing with fewer parts.

problem.practice: Take the most complicated condition in code you own and write its truth table. If it has more than three variables, that is itself the finding — nobody is evaluating it correctly in their head, including whoever wrote it.

beats.broke: Circuit design was an empirical craft of arranging switches until the behaviour looked right, with no way to prove a design correct or reduce it before building it.

beats.cost: Everything above the gates must be expressed in two states, so every quantity a machine handles is a convention layered over two-state storage.
